extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners and patent practitioners (applicants and prosecution attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and documenting obviousness rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103 (including KSR and Graham framework) during patent examination. Covers factual inquiries, search scope, rationales for obviousness, applicant reply and rebuttal, and evidentiary standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory Standard for Obviousness (35 U.S.C. 103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may not be obtained if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made. For applications subject to FITF/AIA use the 'effective filing date' rather than 'time of the invention.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factual inquiries — Scope and content of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining the scope and content of the prior art is a basic factual inquiry in the Graham framework for obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel must first obtain a thorough understanding of the invention by reading the specification (including claims) and give the claims the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification. Once scope is determined, determine what to search for and where to search. See MPEP §904 and §2111.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factual inquiries — Differences between the claimed invention and the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascertaining the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art requires interpreting the claim language and considering both the invention and the prior art as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel must explain why the differences would or would not render the claim nonobvious; the mere existence of differences does not establish nonobviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factual inquiries — Level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art is a factual inquiry and should be included either explicitly or implicitly in view of the prior art applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors to consider include: (1) type of problems encountered in the art; (2) prior art solutions to those problems; (3) rapidity with which innovations are made; (4) sophistication of the technology; (5) educational level of active workers. Examiners may rely on their technical expertise; the hypothetical person is of ordinary creativity, not an automaton.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective evidence / Secondary considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence relevant to obviousness (sometimes called 'secondary considerations') may include commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, and unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such evidence may be in the specification, accompany the application on filing, or be timely submitted later. The weight given is case-by-case; presence of evidence is not dispositive but must be evaluated and articulated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office personnel as factfinders and articulation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel fulfill the role of factfinder for the Graham inquiries and must ensure the written record includes findings of fact concerning the state of the art and the teachings of the references applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once factual findings are articulated, Office personnel must provide an explanation to support an obviousness rejection. Rejections cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; there must be articulated reasoning with a rational underpinning (KSR, In re Kahn). 35 U.S.C. 132 requires informing the applicant of the reasons for rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction — Broadest reasonable interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be given the 'broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification' when determining the scope of the claimed invention for obviousness purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read the specification (including embodiments and disclosure) to understand what has been invented; see Phillips v. AWH and MPEP §2111 for guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search — What to search for
rubrics_metrics.description: The search should cover the claimed subject matter and disclosed features which might reasonably be expected to be claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a rejection need not be based on a teaching/suggestion to combine, a preferred search is directed to finding references that provide such teaching/suggestion if they exist. See MPEP §904.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search — Where to search / Analogous art
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art for 35 U.S.C. 103 can be either in the field of the applicant’s endeavor or reasonably pertinent to the particular problem with which the applicant was concerned (analogous art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art in other fields of endeavor may be considered where design incentives or market forces would prompt predictable variation. Follow general search guidelines in MPEP §904 and see MPEP §2141.01(a) for analogous art discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of level of ordinary skill — applicable factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors that may be considered in determining the level of ordinary skill include problems encountered, prior art solutions, rapidity of innovations, sophistication of technology, and educational level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not every factor must be present; one or more may predominate. Cite cases (In re GPAC, Custom Accessories, Environmental Designs) as needed to justify the level of skill finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of common sense / examiner expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Common sense and ordinary creativity may be invoked in an obviousness analysis, but such invocation must be supported by evidence and a reasoned explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR permits common-sense reasoning but warns against conclusory statements. Where a missing limitation goes to the heart of an invention, reliance on common sense requires particularly strong support (see Arendi v. Apple). Examiners may rely on their technical competence as persons skilled in their fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching-Suggestion-Motivation (TSM) rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: A TSM rationale (teaching, suggestion, or motivation to combine references) is an appropriate rationale if present but should not be applied rigidly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR recognized that TSM captured a helpful insight but rejected an overly formalistic application. If TSM exists, it may support an obviousness rejection; if not, other rationales may suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale — Combining prior art elements with known methods (predictable results)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results may support a conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When combination does no more than yield predictable results, it tends to be obvious (KSR; United States v. Adams, Anderson’s-Black Rock, Sakraida). Use factual findings to show predictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale — Simple substitution of one known element for another
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results can support obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that the substituted element was known and that substitution would have been predictable to a person of ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale — Use of a known technique to improve similar devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a known technique to improve similar devices (methods or products) in the same way may support obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a person of ordinary skill would recognize that a technique used to improve one device would improve similar devices in the same way, using that technique is obvious unless its application is beyond ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale — Applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a known technique to a known device (method, or product) ready for improvement to yield predictable results may support obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate that the device was 'ready for improvement' and that results would have been predictable to one of ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale — 'Obvious to try' with reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Obvious to try' — choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions, with a reasonable expectation of success — can support a finding of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rationale is appropriate where solutions are limited and predictable; it is not sufficient where the path is long, unpredictable, or when there is no reasonable expectation of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale — Known work in one field prompting predictable variations in another
rubrics_metrics.description: Known work in one field of endeavor may prompt variations for use in the same or a different field if the variations would be predictable to one of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider design incentives and market forces; prior art outside the applicant’s field may be analogous when predictable cross-field variation would be expected (KSR).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale — Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art to modify or combine
rubrics_metrics.description: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify or to combine prior art teachings may support obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not required in all cases, identification of such teaching/suggestion/motivation can form a clear rationale; include factual findings explaining how the motivation exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie case requirements — reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie case of obviousness may require a showing that a person of ordinary skill would have had a reasonable expectation of success in pursuing the proposed combination or modification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should articulate why a reasonable expectation exists (or not); lack of reasonable expectation undermines an 'obvious to try' rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness analysis must consider all claim limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: All claim limitations must be considered when making an obviousness determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ignore any limitation; explain how each limitation is taught, suggested, or would have been combined or otherwise rendered predictable to the person of ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant reply requirements (37 CFR 1.111(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the Office action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An effective traverse of factual findings must include a reasoned statement explaining why the Office erred; mere assertion that a prima facie case was not established or that reliance on common knowledge lacks documentary support is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of applicant’s rebuttal evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should consider all timely rebuttal evidence when reevaluating an obviousness determination, including secondary considerations and evidence of unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of evidence that may rebut a combination claim include: (A) technological difficulties preventing combination; (B) elements in combination do not merely perform the same functions they performed separately; (C) results of the claimed combination were unexpected. After rebuttal, reviewers should reconsider the record and confirm continued viability of rejections; follow MPEP §706.07(a) for finality procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art usable under 103 includes prior art under 102 and admissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter that is prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 can be used to support a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103; admitted prior art may be relied upon for both anticipation and obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider admissions as prior art regardless of statutory category; see MPEP §§901–912 and §2141.01 for related discussion.
